I read a study from a psychologist a couple years ago (don't have a link, sorry) that postulated that modern movies and entertainment, with violent themes, fill a critical role in fulfilling instinctive aggressive tendencies, often due to the more mundane and socially restrictive nature of modern society.

He put forward that they act as an imaginative outlet for releasing pent up aggression that couldn't otherwise be fulfilled without facing negative consequences, and rather than harming peoples' psychological state, they could reduce anxiety and frustration, leading to improved cognitive function and stability. Unless there was another underlying mental condition or personality trait that could be aroused or validated through such violent imagery. In which case, such triggers could happen from other avenues other than gaming--although he did concede that gaming could act as a trigger in such circumstances.

He pointed toward the growth of entertainment venues going back to Roman times and concurrent drops in violent acts that can be substantiated through recorded documents. People with such attention consuming access to entertainment were less likely to commit crimes.

It was an interesting read, and although I believe there is more to it than he stated, and the situation is more complicated and person dependent, I am inclined to agree with his argument on some level. As I stated, it was an interesting and novel perspective that is often overlooked in this debate. I wouldn't doubt that he is one of the people critical of the APAs current motivations.

On one hand I would like it for people to acknowledge games can arouse legitimate emotions in people. Games can be a powerful and immersive medium to tell a story.

People should get sad for failing a level and happy for beating it. Whether they are pressing "F" to pay respects or tapping "A" to get back up more quickly. It's more than just pressing buttons, some games are works of art.

On the other hand, I dislike the focus on aggression. Games are made to be exciting! Difficult games can be frustrating because you have to jump very precise, your opponent shot you first and is boasting about it, or you can't figure out the solution to some obscure light puzzle. But once you see all those meat boys from all your tries, throw a lucky grenade and tea-bag xXxYourMumsADragonxXx or get your refund on Journey of the light*, the frustration was a vital part of the experience.

*I added the journey of the light level 1 puzzle as an example of a frustrating puzzle, you can't solve it, the game is a scam. The frustration you get for an unsolvable puzzle should not be the only part of the experience and people who bought it should be refunded.

I've played so many puzzle games that I don't get frustrated any more. Being frustrated just makes it harder for me to think of a solution. The best way is to try to think of something I haven't tried before and don't assume there is a bug in the game.

Yeah, games can definitely arouse aggression, among other emotions. What the APA neglected to mention is how the aggression tends to be short-lived and when tested is yet to show that this aggression is aimed at other people. Frustration is also possible, but the same happens in traditional board games and when building a house of cards. There's no evidence that the interactivity of gaming makes it any different to experiencing violence or sexual imagery in films and TV. What we have is a heavily biased claim with absolutely no evidence, and that's why the open letter was needed.
